title: Africa's digital divide is closing, but participation in the digitalised economy remains highly uneven
authors: Shannon van Wyk-Khosa, Rosevitha Ndumbu, Matthias Krönke
institution: Afrobarometer
verification: Findings summary read at Afrobarometer publication page 2026-11-05; full PDF not read (PDF fetch unsupported).
relevance: Policy Paper 95 from Africa's largest pan-African survey programme (Round 9, 39 countries, 2021-2023 fieldwork) documents the device, electricity and connectivity base that conditions who can participate in AI-era digital economies. Only 18% of respondents own a computer, 47% own a smartphone, 31% use the internet daily, and just 22% of households have grid electricity that works 'all of the time'; on average 42% of citizens have the devices, electricity and internet access needed for the digital economy. Readiness ranges from over 75% in Mauritius, Seychelles, Gabon and Morocco to roughly 10% in Malawi and Madagascar, with men, urban residents, youth and the better-off advantaged. Afrobarometer publishes its microdata openly, and Round 11 (launched 2026) is adding AI-related questions.

title: 50 milhões de brasileiros já usam IA, mas potenciais benefícios continuam limitados às camadas de maior renda e escolaridade (TIC Domicílios 2025)
authors: Cetic.br / NIC.br (CGI.br)
institution: Cetic.br, NIC.br / CGI.br (Brazil)
verification: Findings summary read at Cetic.br news page 2026-11-05; full TIC Domicílios 2025 report not read.
relevance: First edition of Brazil's national ICT household survey (running since 2005) to include generative-AI indicators: fieldwork March-August 2025, 27,177 households and 24,535 individuals, in-person interviews in urban and rural areas. The authors report that 32% of Brazilian internet users used generative AI (about 50 million people aged 10+), but use is 69% in class A vs 16% in classes D/E, and 59% among the tertiary-educated vs 17% among primary-educated; 86% of students used AI for school research or coursework, and 65% of non-users with only primary education cited lack of skill. The survey quantifies an income- and education-stratified AI participation gap in a major emerging economy, with open microdata published by Cetic.br.

title: People's Attitudes and Perceptions in Qatar Towards Artificial Intelligence Technologies
authors: Mustafa Altıntaş, Mustafa Selman Yaylalı, Muhammed Ali Topal
institution: Qatar University (chapter in 'Shaping the Future of Development in the GCC', Palgrave Macmillan / Gulf Research Center Cambridge)
verification: Abstract read at Springer chapter page 2026-11-05; full text paywalled. Sample size and recruitment not stated in the abstract.
relevance: A rare peer-reviewed Gulf-region survey of public AI attitudes, filling a Middle East gap in the map. The authors find generally optimistic views of AI for economic gains and personal productivity alongside concerns about privacy, job loss, over-reliance, and regulatory gaps; respondents with low interest in AI hold significantly fewer positive attitudes, Qatari nationals worry less about AI risks than non-Qataris, and younger participants are more confident that AI is adequately regulated. Open-ended answers name healthcare, education and transportation as the sectors most likely to benefit.

title: 第4回「AIに関する生活者意識調査」(Dentsu AI-related Consumer Awareness Survey, 4th wave)
authors: Dentsu Inc. (fieldwork by Dentsu Macromill Insight)
institution: Dentsu (Japan)
verification: Release summary read at Dentsu press release (Japanese) 2026-11-05.
relevance: Japan's largest recurring consumer AI survey (4th wave): online survey of 3,000 AI-service users aged 15-69, fielded 7-9 November 2025. The authors report that 61.7% have vague expectations of AI services and the same share have been satisfied with AI-generated content quality, but only 60.0% of 15-19-year-olds trust AI information (lowest of all age groups) despite 70.7% of them fact-checking AI answers; 64.0% overall have experienced AI giving wrong answers. 26.3% have bought a product recommended by AI, and 63.4% of company employees say AI improved work efficiency - a useful non-Western counterpoint to US/European attitude surveys, showing high adoption combined with youth scepticism.

title: The scale of artificial intelligence literacy for all (SAIL4ALL): assessing knowledge of artificial intelligence in all adult populations
authors: María T. Soto-Sanfiel, Ariadna Angulo-Brunet, Christoph Lutz
institution: Hamad Bin Khalifa University (Qatar) with University of Barcelona and BI Norwegian Business School; Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
verification: Abstract and method summary read at Nature article page 2026-11-05; full text not read.
relevance: Peer-reviewed psychometric instrument for measuring factual AI literacy in the general adult population, built on Long and Magerko's framework in three phases (expert item rating; UK pilot n=501; two UK Prolific samples n=619 and n=393) to a final 56-item scale covering 'What is AI?', 'What can AI do?', 'How does AI work?' and 'How should AI be used?'. The authors report good fit (CFI/TLI >= 0.90 mostly), better internal consistency in Likert than true/false formats, and gender/education differences: men scored higher on recognising AI use and how AI works, and higher-educated participants scored higher on most dimensions. Stated limitations include UK-only samples, Prolific self-selection, and possible ceiling effects - so it still needs cross-cultural validation, but it is a ready-made open measure for comparative AI-literacy studies.

title: Citizens and Experts Unite: Final Report on Global Consultations for France's 2025 AI Action Summit
authors: The Future Society, CNNum, Make.org, Sciences Po Tech & Global Affairs, AI & Society Institute (ENS-PSL)
institution: The Future Society and partners (for the Paris AI Action Summit)
verification: Executive summary read at The Future Society report page 2026-11-05; 118-page PDF not read.
relevance: The largest documented global citizen consultation on AI governance to date: 10,000+ citizens and 200+ experts worldwide consulted between September and December 2024 to feed the Paris AI Action Summit, described by the organisers as the first such engagement in an AI summit's preparation. Participants converged on five priorities - multistakeholder global governance including an international scientific cooperation body on AI risks, shared safety standards with corporate commitment report cards, universal AI education and critical thinking, environmental sustainability standards, and public-interest AI in healthcare, climate and anti-disinformation. The authors characterise the overall stance as 'constructive vigilance': targeted deployment where value is proven and risks managed, rather than blanket rollout.

title: AI Diffusion in Low Resource Language Countries
authors: Amit Misra, Syed Waqas Zamir, Wassim Hamidouche, Inbal Becker-Reshef, Juan Lavista Ferres
institution: University of Maryland and Microsoft (arXiv preprint)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full text not read.
relevance: Quantitative test of the claim that language is an independent barrier to AI inclusion: using a weighted regression that isolates the language effect from socioeconomic and demographic confounders, the authors find that countries dominated by low-resource languages have an AI-user share approximately 20% lower than their baseline characteristics would predict. The mechanism proposed is frontier LLM underperformance on low-resource languages due to training-data scarcity, which lowers practical utility and dampens adoption. Directly relevant to 'who is heard' - most of the world's ~7,000 languages are low-resource, so the paper links model coverage to measurable participation gaps.

title: Digital News Report 2025
authors: Nic Newman et al. (Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism)
institution: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, University of Oxford
verification: Executive summary read at Reuters Institute page 2026-11-05; full 171-page PDF not read.
relevance: The 14th edition of the largest global news-attitude survey (48 markets across six continents, including India, Brazil, Nigeria and other non-Western markets). The authors report that 58% worry about distinguishing true from false news online; weekly AI-chatbot use for news is 7% overall but 15% among under-25s and 18% in India vs 3% in the UK; audiences remain sceptical of fully AI-generated news, with net expectations that AI will make news cheaper (+29) but less trustworthy (-18), and comfort with AI-generated news varying from 44% in India to 11% in the UK. Also documents 22% of Apple News users' AI-summarised alerts being withdrawn after inaccuracies - a concrete trust/misuse datapoint.

title: Global State of Scams - 2025
authors: Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA)
institution: Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA)
verification: Landing-page summary read at GASA 2026-11-05; full report is members-only and the landing page does not itself list AI-specific scam figures (AI-powered tactics such as deepfakes and voice cloning are covered in the full report per partner coverage).
relevance: The broadest recurring measurement of scam victimisation, covering 46,000 adults across 42 markets - including Asian, African and Latin American economies usually absent from fraud surveys. The landing page reports that seven in ten adults globally encountered a scam in the last 12 months and 13% encounter scams at least once a day. The full (members-only) report covers AI-enabled tactics such as deepfakes, voice cloning and generative phishing, making this the closest global baseline for AI-assisted fraud exposure; GASA also publishes national spin-offs (e.g., State of Scams in Indonesia with Mastercard).

title: The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
authors: Kobi Hackenburg, Ben M. Tappin, Luke Hewitt, Ed Saunders, Sid Black, Hause Lin, Catherine Fist, Helen Margetts, David G. Rand, Christopher Summerfield
institution: University of Oxford (OII) and collaborators; published in Science
verification: Abstract read at arXiv preprint version (arXiv:2507.13919) 2026-11-05; the Science version is paywalled and was not read.
relevance: Large-scale peer-reviewed experiment on AI's persuasion capabilities: 19 LLMs deployed on 707 political issues with 76,977 participants, plus fact-checking of 466,769 AI-generated claims. The authors find AI-generated messages can be more persuasive than human-written ones, and that persuasive power comes mainly from post-training on persuasive data (up to +51%) and prompting strategies (up to +27%) rather than model scale or personalisation - and, strikingly, that more persuasive outputs were systematically less factually accurate. The authors conclude such capability is within reach of large and small actors alike, with direct implications for elections and information integrity.

title: iProov Study Reveals Deepfake Blindspot: Only 0.1% of People Can Accurately Detect AI-Generated Deepfakes
authors: iProov
institution: iProov (industry research)
verification: Press release with study details read at iProov 2026-11-05; the study is industry research, not peer-reviewed.
relevance: Experimental test of deepfake-detection ability in 2,000 UK and US consumers shown real and AI-generated images and videos, with participants primed to look for fakes: only 0.1% correctly identified every stimulus, and synthetic videos were 36% harder to spot than synthetic images. The authors also report an awareness gap (22% had never heard of deepfakes; 39% among those 65+), overconfidence (over 60% confident regardless of accuracy), and behavioural consequences (49% trust social media less; 74% worry about societal impact, with misinformation the top concern at 68%). Useful as a headline misuse statistic, with the stated caveat that it is vendor-funded research.

title: A community-codesigned LLM-powered chatbot for primary care: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Sairan Li, Yanzeng Li, Shuya Zhou, ... Lei Zou, Shasha Han (Peking Union Medical College, Peking University, University of Glasgow, Tencent WeChat AI)
institution: Peking Union Medical College / CAMS and collaborators; Nature Health
verification: Full-text summary read at PubMed Central 2026-11-05.
relevance: Pragmatic double-blinded RCT (ChiCTR2500098101) of 'P&P Care', an LLM primary-care chatbot codesigned with community stakeholders via a dual-track role-play framework: 2,202 randomised and 2,113 analysed across urban and rural communities in 11 Chinese provinces (59.1% rural), comparing consultation plus e-learning modules vs consultation alone. The primary endpoint of objective health-need awareness was met (2.95 vs 2.34, P<0.001), all five consultation-quality metrics favoured the e-learning arm, and the chatbot outperformed recorded usual-care and telemedicine benchmarks on history-taking and diagnosis (4.13 vs 2.86 and 2.30). Authors state limitations honestly: no live usual-care control, unmonitored e-learning adherence, smaller gains among rural participants, and possible under-serving of some of China's 200+ dialects.

title: Large language model diagnostic assistance for physicians in a lower-middle-income country: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Imran Ahmed Qazi, Ali Ali, Ayesha U. Khawaja, M. Jahangeer Akhtar, A. Z. Sheikh, M. H. Alizai
institution: Pakistan-based research team (multi-institution); Nature Health
verification: Abstract-level summary read at Nature article page 2026-11-05 (open access); full text not read.
relevance: Randomised trial (NCT06774612) testing whether GPT-4o access improves diagnostic reasoning for 60 licensed physicians in Pakistan - a rare LMIC setting for clinical AI evidence. After a 20-hour AI-literacy curriculum, physicians with LLM access scored 71.4% vs 42.6% for conventional resources alone (adjusted difference 27.5 percentage points, 95% CI 22.8-32.2, P<0.001) with no time penalty, and gains were largest for less-experienced physicians (+30.0 pp) and those with little prior LLM use (+46.4 pp). Notably, GPT-4o alone scored 82.9%, above physician+LLM, and the authors flag vignette-only design, a single model, and inability to separate curriculum effects from LLM-access effects as limitations.

title: How AI is used in FDA-authorized medical devices: a taxonomy across 1,016 authorizations
authors: Rohan Singh, Monika Bapna, Abdul Rahman Diab, Emily S. Ruiz, William Lotter
institution: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Brigham and Women's Hospital / Harvard Medical School; npj Digital Medicine
verification: Full-text summary read at Nature article page 2026-11-05 (open access).
relevance: Manual classification of all 1,016 FDA authorizations of AI/ML-enabled medical devices listed as of 20 December 2024 (grouped into 736 unique devices) - the most complete public map of what deployed clinical AI actually does. The authors report images dominate (621 devices, 84.4%, mostly radiology), 85.6% of devices do analysis vs 11.3% generation, quantification/feature-localisation is the largest AI function (65% of analysis devices) but is declining as a share (81% of new devices in 2016 to 51% in 2024) while triage and image enhancement grow, and no LLM-based devices appear on the list. Limitations stated: reliance on variable public summaries, some inferred classifications, and FDA's broad AI/ML definition including traditional ML.

title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
authors: Greg Kestin, Kelly Miller, Anna Klales, Timothy Milbourne, Gregorio Ponti
institution: Harvard University; Scientific Reports
verification: Full-text summary read at Nature article page 2026-11-05 (open access).
relevance: Randomised crossover trial in Harvard's Physical Sciences 2 course (N=194 of 233 enrolled, Fall 2023) comparing a custom GPT-4-based tutor with pedagogical guardrails against the same course's in-class active-learning lessons. Students learned more than twice as much in less time with the AI tutor (median post-test 4.5 vs 3.5, p<10^-8; regression effect size 0.63 SD, quantile regression 0.73-1.3 SD) and reported higher engagement (4.1 vs 3.6) and motivation, with 83% rating AI explanations as good as or better than human instructors'. The authors explicitly caution against AI replacing class time: results cover initial learning at understanding/applying levels, depended on instructor-written solutions to limit hallucinations, and higher-order synthesis was not assessed.

title: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria
authors: Martin De Simone, Federico Tiberti, Maria Barron Rodriguez, Federico Manolio, Wuraola Mosuro, Eliot Jolomi Dikoru
institution: World Bank (Policy Research Working Paper No. 11125)
verification: Abstract read at World Bank Open Knowledge Repository 2026-11-05; full 51-page PDF not read.
relevance: One of the first RCTs of generative AI as a school tutor in a developing country: a six-week after-school programme using Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) for English learning among first-year senior secondary students in Nigeria. The authors report an overall 0.31 SD improvement on assessments covering Nigerian-curriculum English, AI knowledge and digital skills (0.23 SD on English alone), equivalent to 1.5-2 years of business-as-usual schooling, with benefits across the ability distribution and the largest gains for female students and higher performers - and among the most cost-effective education interventions evaluated. A reproducibility package is published alongside the paper (CC BY 3.0 IGO).
